module.title: Correct Mechanics for Issuing a Card
objectives: Name the cautionable and sending-off offences in Law 12
Apply the careless, reckless and excessive force test to a challenge
Run the four-step carding mechanic without having to think about it
Display a card so the player, both benches and all observers see it
Decide when the card is shown under advantage or a quick free kick
Record the incident so it can be acted on in a Match Report

pages.title: Correct Mechanics for Issuing a Card

blocks.transcript: Every referee carries two cards. What separates a confident official from an uncertain one is not whether they are willing to use them. It is whether the picture they present when they do is clear enough that nobody watching has to guess what just happened. This module is about that picture.

body: In this lesson you will learn to identify misconduct under Law 12, decide between no card, a caution and a send-off, and display the card so that the player, both benches and every observer understand the decision.
A card shown badly costs you more than a card shown late. The Law tells you what to punish. The mechanic is what makes it stick.

blocks.heading: By the end of this module you will be able to:
items: Name the cautionable and sending-off offences in Law 12
Apply the careless, reckless and excessive force test to a challenge
Run the four-step carding mechanic without having to think about it
Display a card so the player, both benches and all observers see it
Decide when the card is shown under advantage or a quick free kick
Record the incident so it can be acted on in a Match Report

blocks.transcript: A foul and a misconduct are not the same thing. Most of the fouls you call carry no card at all. Misconduct is the smaller set of offences the Law says must be punished with a caution or a send-off — and it does not wait for the ball to be in play.

body: Every misconduct is punished with a card. Not every foul is a misconduct.
Misconduct can occur at any time, including when the ball is out of play, and before kick-off or after the final whistle. It can be committed by a player, a substitute, or a substituted player.

slides.title: A foul is not a card.
slides.imageBrief: Referee awarding a free kick, no card in hand.
slides.body: You will call fifteen to thirty fouls in a typical youth match. Most end with a free kick and nothing else. Reaching for a card on a foul that doesn't require one spends credibility you'll need later.

slides.title: The ball does not have to be in play.
slides.imageBrief: Two players squaring up during a stoppage.
slides.body: Dissent during a drinks break. A shove at a throw-in. An elbow off the ball while a corner is set. Each is misconduct, and each is cautionable or worse — even though play had stopped.

slides.title: It is not only the eleven on the field.
slides.body: Substitutes and substituted players are subject to the same offences. A substitute who dissents from the bench is cautioned exactly as a player on the field would be.

items.label: CAUTIONABLE OFFENCES — Yellow card
bullets: Unsporting behaviour — the widest category: a reckless challenge, a tactical shirt pull, simulation, a provoking celebration.
Dissent by word or action — disputing the decision, not disliking it.
Persistent offences — a pattern, not a count. There is no magic number in Law 12.
Entering, re-entering or deliberately leaving the field without permission.
Failing to respect the required distance at a restart.

items.label: SENDING-OFF OFFENCES — Red card
items.intro: A player, substitute or substituted player is sent off for:
bullets: Serious foul play — a challenge for the ball using excessive force or endangering safety.
Violent conduct — force or attempted force when not contesting the ball.
Offensive, insulting or abusive language or actions.
Denying a goal or an obvious goal-scoring opportunity (handball, or an offence).
Receiving a second caution in the same match.

blocks.prompt: Twenty minutes into a U15 match, play is stopped for a throw-in. A defender you've already spoken to once walks past you and says, loudly, “That's the third one you've missed.” What is this?

options.text: Nothing. The ball is out of play, so Law 12 does not apply.
A foul. Restart with an indirect free kick.
Misconduct. Dissent by word, and it is cautionable.
Misconduct, but you can only deal with it at half time.

blocks.lesson: Misconduct applies whenever you have jurisdiction, in play or out of it. Dissent by word or action is cautionable, and a stoppage is the best moment to deal with it.

blocks.transcript: Here is the decision that sits underneath every card you'll ever show for a challenge. Law 12 gives you three levels, and the level you choose decides the sanction for you. Careless is a free kick. Reckless must be a caution. Excessive force must be a send-off. The word must matters.

rows: A lack of attention or consideration, or acting without precaution
Disregard to the danger to, or consequences for, an opponent
Direct free kick. Must be cautioned.
Exceeds necessary force, or endangers an opponent's safety
Direct free kick. Must be sent off.

cards.title: CARELESS
cards.body: Mistimed. The player was going for the ball and got it wrong.

cards.title: RECKLESS
cards.body: The player knew, or should have known, this could hurt someone, and went anyway.

cards.title: EXCESSIVE FORCE
cards.body: More force than the challenge needed, or the opponent's safety put at risk.

blocks.heading: What you are actually reading
body: Speed. Intensity. Distance into the challenge. Whether the player was in control. Whether the studs were showing. Whether contact was with the ball or the opponent.
Those are the inputs. Do not add “was anyone hurt” to the list. Injury is evidence, not a level.

blocks.clipBrief: A side-on challenge. The player wins the ball cleanly, then follows through into the opponent's shin at moderate speed.

options.text: Careless, no card
Reckless, yellow
Excessive force, red

blocks.lesson: Winning the ball first does not downgrade the challenge. The follow-through showed disregard for the consequences. Free kick and a caution.

blocks.clipBrief: A player stretches for a loose ball, arrives late, light contact, low speed, under control throughout.

options.text: Careless, no card
Reckless, yellow
Excessive force, red

blocks.lesson: Late and clumsy, but controlled and slow. Free kick and, if you want, a word. Carding this is the most common over-reach in youth football.

blocks.clipBrief: A player lunges in from distance, both feet off the ground, studs showing, at pace.

options.text: Careless, no card
Reckless, yellow
Excessive force, red

blocks.lesson: Speed, distance, no control, studs showing. Safety endangered. Serious foul play — the player is sent off.

blocks.prompt: A midfielder makes a committed, high-speed challenge from the side with studs showing. The opponent sees it coming, jumps clear, and is untouched. What do you have?

options.text: Nothing. No contact, so no foul.
A free kick only. No contact means no card.
A red card for serious foul play. The challenge endangered the opponent's safety.
A yellow card. Without contact it can't be more than reckless.

blocks.lesson: Law 12 judges the challenge, not the outcome. A challenge made with excessive force, or one that endangers safety, is serious foul play whether or not it connects.

blocks.transcript: MOD1 gave you a four-step model. Here is what it looks like when the decision is a card. These are not steps you work through consciously in the moment — they are the habit you build, so the sequence runs on its own and you don't skip the step that matters most. For carding, that's almost always the third one.

items.label: SEE
items.heading: See the Incident
items.body: Observe the offence from an angle that isn't blocked. If you didn't see it cleanly, admit that to yourself and check your assistant. A card shown on a guess is a card you can't defend.

items.label: RECOGNIZE
items.heading: Recognize the Offence
items.body: Name it in your head in the words Law 12 uses. Reckless challenge. Dissent by word. Second caution. Naming it tells you which card to reach for — and is the phrase you'll need when the coach asks and when you write the report.

items.label: THINK
items.heading: Think About the Picture
items.body: This is the step officials skip. Before you move, settle three things: who the player is (number and face), where you'll stand so this can be seen, and whether anything has to settle first. Ten seconds here saves ten minutes later.

items.label: ACT
items.heading: Act With Control
items.body: Isolate the player, establish eye contact, show the card clearly and high, and record it before you restart. Controlled by default; quicker only where speed prevents retaliation.

blocks.prompt: Think back to the last card you showed. Which of the four steps got the least of your attention in that moment? Write a sentence about what you'd do differently.
blocks.followUp: There's no wrong answer. Most referees name Think — the only one of the four that asks you to slow down at the exact moment everyone around you is speeding up.

blocks.transcript: The decision is made. Now comes the part the Law calls presenting the correct picture. When the card goes up, the offending player knows it's for them, both coaching staffs know who it's for, and every observer can see something has been dealt with. If any one of those three is in doubt, the card didn't do its job.

blocks.imageBrief: Referee walking in on a group of players in front of the technical area.
lines: Second half. U16 boys. The score is 1–1 and the home bench has been loud for twenty minutes.
A midfielder catches his opponent late, off the ball, right in front of the benches. I see it clearly. It is reckless. It is a caution.
Four players arrive before I do. Two of them are shouting at each other. The home coach is already off his seat.
I have the card in my hand. The question is not whether to show it. The question is when, where, and to whom.

slides.title: 1. Stop play and signal the restart first.
slides.body: Blow, then signal the restart. The players need to know play is dead. Pointing the direction first also buys you three seconds to think.

slides.title: 2. Move in. Don't card from distance.
slides.body: Walk towards the incident at a steady pace. A card shown from twenty-five yards reads as a referee who didn't want to deal with it.

slides.title: 3. Separate before you sanction.
slides.body: If there's a crowd or a confrontation, deal with that first. A card shown into a group of eight adds fuel to the thing you're trying to put out.

slides.title: 4. Identify and isolate the player.
slides.body: Confirm the number and the face. Move the player two or three steps clear of the group.

slides.title: 5. Set your distance and angle.
slides.body: About an arm's length and a half away, square to the player, with the benches and most spectators in view behind them.

slides.title: 6. Show the card high and still.
slides.body: Eye contact first. Then the card goes up above your head height, held still for a full second. Vertical and still. Never pointed, never waved.

slides.title: 7. Record it, then restart.
slides.body: Notebook out before you walk away. Number, time, offence.

blocks.prompt: Three of these referees have the mechanic wrong. Choose the one who has it right.

options.imageBrief: Card at waist height, referee already walking away.
options.optionFallbackText: Card at waist height, referee already walking away, player behind him
options.feedback: Wrong. The player can't see it and neither can the benches.

options.imageBrief: Card held high and still, square to an isolated player, benches behind.
options.optionFallbackText: Card held high and still, square to an isolated player, benches visible behind
options.feedback: Correct. Player, both benches and the crowd all see it.

options.imageBrief: Card pointed into the player's face.
options.optionFallbackText: Card pointed into the player's face at close range
options.feedback: Wrong. Aggressive. Turns a sanction into a confrontation.

options.imageBrief: Card held up inside a group of six.
options.optionFallbackText: Card held up inside a group of six players
options.feedback: Wrong. No isolation. Nobody knows who it's for.

items.label: Carding the wrong player
items.body: The most damaging error available to you. Confirm number and face; if unsure, ask your assistant first. A card withdrawn costs far more than a card delayed.

items.label: Pointing the card
items.body: The card is displayed, not aimed. Pointing invites a response.

items.label: Showing it and not recording it
items.body: You will misremember. Write it down before the restart.

items.label: Over-explaining
items.body: One short sentence naming the offence, then stop. The longer you talk, the more you invite an argument.

blocks.heading: Every card has a consequence
body: A yellow card doesn't remove the player, but it changes the match for them: any further misconduct ends their afternoon and leaves their team short.
A red card removes the player immediately. They must leave the field, and the team plays short for the rest of the match.

blocks.prompt: You've decided to caution number 9. Six players are around the incident and two of them are shouting at each other. What do you do first?

options.text: Show the card immediately, so everyone sees it's dealt with.
Step in, separate the two players, let the group settle, then isolate number 9 and caution.
Move away and caution number 9 at the next stoppage.
Caution number 9 from where you stand, then deal with the two shouting.

blocks.lesson: Sanctioning into a live confrontation adds to it. Control, then isolate, then show the card where it can be seen. The caution isn't going anywhere — play can't restart until it's administered.

blocks.transcript: The decision to punish misconduct is made at the moment the offence is committed. When the card is physically shown is a separate question, and the Law gives you several answers depending on what's happening around you.

blocks.heading: The default
body: Once you've decided to caution or send off a player, play must not restart until the sanction has been administered. Everything below is an exception to that one rule.

nodes.text: An offence is committed that carries a card.

branches.to: Sanction at the next stoppage — with DOGSO / promising-attack exceptions
Was a quick free kick taken before you started the procedure?

nodes.text: Advantage → sanction when the ball is next out of play.
exceptions: DOGSO offence + a goal resulted → no sanction.
DOGSO offence + no goal → caution for unsporting behaviour (not a send-off).
Stopped a promising attack → no caution.

nodes.text: Quick free kick with a clear chance, procedure not started → allow it; card at the next stoppage.
Otherwise → administer the sanction now, before the restart.

blocks.prompt: A defender trips an attacker through on goal. You play advantage, the move continues, and a different attacker scores five seconds later. What happens to the defender?

options.text: Sent off for denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity.
Cautioned for unsporting behaviour.
No sanction.
Cautioned, but only if he was the last defender.

blocks.lesson: When advantage is played for a DOGSO offence and the advantage results in a goal, there is no sanction. The team got the thing the offence tried to take from them.

blocks.title: Reference table
rows: Offence carrying a card, play stopped

blocks.transcript: The card is shown, the game restarts, and ninety seconds later you're thinking about something else entirely. That's exactly why you write it down before you restart.

body: Record the incident at the moment it happens, before play restarts. Not at half time. Not afterwards.

blocks.heading: Record every card with:
items: The offence, in the words Law 12 uses
What the player actually did, in one plain sentence
Where on the field it happened
Whether it was a first or second caution

cards.title: Strong
cards.body: “63rd minute. Blue No. 6. Caution, unsporting behaviour. Reckless challenge from the side on Red No. 11 near the halfway line. Studs showing, follow-through to the shin. No attempt to withdraw.”

blocks.prompt: Go back to the page-4 scenario. The midfielder catches his opponent late, off the ball, in front of the benches, 58th minute. He is Blue No. 14. Write the line you'd put in your notebook.
blocks.followUp: Compare yours against the strong example above. Did you name the offence in Law 12's words? Did you describe what he did, not only what you called it?

blocks.prompt: When should the incident be recorded?

options.text: At half time, while it's still fresh.
Before play restarts.
At the final whistle, with the rest of the match details.
Only if the card was a red.

blocks.lesson: Record before the restart. Memory degrades quickly under match load. Every misconduct gets recorded — yellow and red alike.

setup: U17 boys, state cup quarter-final. 71st minute. The score is 2–2.

A long ball goes over the top. Blue No. 4 and Red No. 9 both chase it, forty yards from Blue's goal and drifting towards the touchline. Blue No. 4 arrives late and takes Red No. 9 down from behind with a trailing leg.
Red No. 9 stays down. Two Red players are already running at me. The Blue bench is shouting that the ball was gone.

options.text: Careless. Free kick, no card.
options.feedback: The trailing leg caught him from behind, at speed, with no attempt to play a ball that had already gone. You've under-read the level — and told both teams this challenge is available for the rest of the match.

options.text: Reckless. Free kick, caution.
options.feedback: Right level. From behind, at speed, with disregard for the consequences. A caution for unsporting behaviour.

options.text: Excessive force. Free kick, send off.
options.feedback: Worth considering, but check your inputs. Late and from behind — but was there excessive force, and was safety endangered? If speed and follow-through were moderate, reckless is the level.

decisions.prompt: Two Red players have arrived, and one is standing over Blue No. 4. What do you do first?

options.text: Show the yellow now, so the matter is visibly dealt with.
options.feedback: You show the card into a live confrontation. The two Red players read it as vindication and close in; the Blue bench reads it as bias. Now you have a second problem on top of the first.

options.text: Step in, separate, check on the injured player, then isolate No. 4 and caution.
options.feedback: Control first, sanction second. The caution can't be lost — play can't restart until it's administered — so there's no hurry.

options.text: Move away and caution at the next stoppage.
options.feedback: Play is already stopped. There is no next stoppage, and walking away with the sanction owed reads as indecision.

decisions.prompt: You've isolated Blue No. 4. Where do you stand, and how do you show it?

options.text: Close, facing the player, card at chest height.
options.feedback: Too close and too low. The benches can't see it, and the proximity invites a response.

options.text: An arm's length and a half away, square to the player, card high and still above head height, benches in view.
options.feedback: The player sees it. Both benches see it. The spectators see it. Hold it still for a full second.

options.text: Beside the player, card raised while already turning to the restart.
options.feedback: Half the ground missed it, and you'll be asked to explain a decision that should have explained itself.

close: You hold the card for a second. Then the notebook: 71st minute, Blue No. 4, caution, unsporting behaviour, reckless challenge from behind on Red No. 9 near the touchline.
You check on Red No. 9, confirm he can continue, and restart with the direct free kick.
The Blue bench is still unhappy. That's fine. Everyone in the ground knows exactly what happened and who it happened to. That is what the mechanic is for.

blocks.heading: Recap
blocks.intro: Law 12 gives you three steps. Everything in this module sits inside them.
items: Identify the offence. Name it in the Law's own words, and name the level: careless, reckless, or excessive force.
Stop play and clearly display the proper card. Isolate, set your distance, make eye contact, card high and still.
Record the decision for the official report. Before the restart, not after.

items.prompt: Dissent during a throw-in stoppage is…
options: Not punishable — ball out of play

items.prompt: A reckless challenge that misses the opponent is…
A late, slow, controlled challenge is usually…
A high-speed, studs-up challenge that the opponent jumps clear of is…
Carding into a live confrontation is…
Advantage played on a DOGSO offence, no goal results →
The card is shown so that…
options: The player, both benches and observers all see it
